newsitem.title: USA: U.S. strongly backs new Mexican drug czar.
newsitem.headline: U.S. strongly backs new Mexican drug czar.

text.p: The United States on Monday threw its strong support behind Mexico's new anti-drug czar and said the appointment strengthened President Bill Clinton's case for designating Mexico an ally in the war on drugs.
Mariano Herran Salvatti, a little known lawyer, was named by President Ernesto Zedillo to head Mexico's war on drugs.
He replaces Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, a distinguished military officer who was abruptly jailed on charges he was in the pay of Amado Carrillo Fuentes, Mexico's top drug lord.

The Gutierrez scandal caused an uproar in Washington, where members of Congress said it showed how far traffickers had penetrated Mexican government institutions, and deeply embarrassed President Zedillo.
"We think it's a highly significant appointment which ought to be welcomed by the detractors of our president's policy," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

"We have absolute trust and confidence in President Zedillo...He has chosen this man personally. It's obviously, an exceedingly important appointment in the wake of the resignation of Mr. Salvatti's predecessor."

Burns said he hoped the announcement "will convince those in Congress and those around the country and perhaps even in our own hemisphere who have any doubts that President's Zedillo's commitment to wage the war against narcotics is genuine."

The spokesman noted that it had been difficult for Zedillo to have his former drug czar under suspicion of working with the cartels and the appointment "means that we can get back to business with Mexico on the experts' level to make sure that we're cooperating very closely with the Mexican government."
The appointment also "strengthens the case of the administration that we've got to move forward with this certification decision and not change it," Burns said.

As part of an annual exercise mandated by Congress, Clinton recently re-certified Mexico as an ally in the war against illegal narcotics despite claims of corruption in Mexico's government and lack of cooperation among law enforcement agencies.
A U.S. House of Representatives committee voted last week to overturn Clinton's certification finding and the full House is to vote later this week.

Zedillo, under heavy pressure from Washington to show results in the drug war, has declared the fight against the traffickers who smuggle tons of cocaine, marijuana and heroin across the border into the United States each year, to be Mexico's top national security priority.
A team of three senior administration officials was in Mexico for talks last week. Clinton and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright are to visit Mexico on April 11-12.
